issues.legal_issue: The residence-based succession provision for a deceased tenant does not make a family member a tenant of business premises merely because that member resided with the deceased tenant.
material_facts: The original tenant died while eviction litigation concerning a shop was pending.
The tenant’s son was impleaded and claimed tenancy as a member of the deceased tenant’s family.
issues.conclusion: The family member could not claim tenancy of the business premises under the residence-based succession provision.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(11)(c) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, was construed as protecting family members residing with a deceased tenant in relation to residential premises, not business premises. The Court approved Parubai Manilal Brahmin v. Baldevdas Zaverbhai Tapodhan and overruled Heirs of Deceased Darji Mohanlal Lavji v. Muktabai Shamji. The Court also treated the later Gujarat legislative distinction between residential premises and business premises as supporting that construction, while noting that it did not govern interpretation of the Maharashtra provision.

predicates.business_premises_tenancy_succession_cla: A person claims tenancy succession to premises used for business after the tenant dies.
predicates.family_member_claims_through_residence_w: The claimant relies on being a member of the deceased tenant’s family who resided with the tenant.

issues.definition: When a family member claims succession to a deceased tenant’s business premises solely through residence with the deceased tenant, the family member does not become a tenant under a residence-based succession rule.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who does not strictly comply with the conditions for alternative protection from eviction for rent default cannot receive discretionary relief under that protection.
material_facts: The landlord brought an eviction suit based on unpaid rent.
The standard rent had been disputed, and the Trial Court treated the alternative protection provision as applicable rather than the provision requiring a decree upon satisfaction of its conditions.
The tenant did not pay rent regularly in accordance with the conditions for the alternative protection.
The appellate court held that the statutory conditions had not been complied with.
issues.conclusion: The alternative protection provision created no discretion to excuse the tenant’s failure to meet its conditions; where those conditions were not met, an eviction decree had to follow if no other protection applied.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 12(3)(a) and 12(3)(b) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, a decree is obligatory when the conditions of section 12(3)(a) are satisfied. If they are not satisfied, section 12(3)(b) gives the tenant an opportunity to defeat eviction by strictly meeting its conditions, including regular payment or tender of rent as required. The provision creates no discretionary jurisdiction to relieve a tenant who fails to comply. The Court relied on Shah Dhansukhlal Chhaganlal v. Dalichand Firchand Shroff and Harbanslal Jagmohandas v. Prabhudas Shivlal, and referred to Hatilal Balabhai Nazar v. Ranchodbhai Shankarbhai Patel on the mandatory effect of section 12(3)(a). It overruled Kalidas v. Bhavan Bhagwandas to the extent that it treated the provision as conferring discretion.

predicates.rent_default_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brings a proceeding seeking eviction because the tenant has defaulted in paying rent.
predicates.alternative_payment_protection_applies: The case falls within a statutory alternative that lets a tenant avoid eviction by meeting specified payment conditions.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_meet_payment_conditions: The tenant does not make the payments or tenders required to obtain that alternative protection.

issues.definition: In a rent-default eviction proceeding, if the tenant’s protection depends on meeting specified payment conditions and the tenant fails to meet them, an eviction decree is required.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction may not disturb a subordinate court’s factual finding unless it is clearly perverse or patently unreasonable.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the appellate court’s eviction judgment through a petition invoking the High Court’s supervisory jurisdiction.
The appellate court had found that the Trial Court’s exercise of discretion was proper, even on the view that discretion existed.
The High Court allowed the petition without considering or setting aside that finding.
The relevant finding about the circumstances was a finding of fact and was not shown to be clearly perverse or patently unreasonable.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s interference was unwarranted, and its judgment was set aside in favour of the appellate court’s judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution do not authorize the High Court to reweigh or interfere with subordinate-court findings of fact merely because it might reach a different view. Interference is unavailable unless the finding is clearly perverse or patently unreasonable; supervisory jurisdiction is limited to ensuring that the subordinate court acts within its authority. The Court relied on Babhutmal Raichand Oswal v. Laxmibai R. Tarte.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_subordinate_court_: A party asks a High Court to review a subordinate court’s decision through supervisory jurisdiction.
predicates.subordinate_court_made_factual_finding: The subordinate court made a finding based on the facts or circumstances of the case.
predicates.finding_not_clearly_perverse_or_patently: The factual finding is not clearly perverse or patently unreasonable.

issues.definition: In supervisory review, when a subordinate court has made a factual finding that is not clearly perverse or patently unreasonable, the High Court must not interfere with that finding.
